name: Matterport on AI in Real Estate and Property Management
title: Matterport on AI in Real Estate and Property Management
answer: Matterport, the 3D capture and digital twin company, publishes blog posts on AI in real estate and property management. Its most useful single claim is a cited Delta Media figure that over 87% of brokerages actively use AI tools, up 7% in the past year. The posts also distinguish generative AI, which creates listing descriptions and virtual staging, from agentic AI, which acts autonomously, and describe Property Intelligence tools that automate listing tasks from 3D property scans.

sections.body: Matterport, a company known for 3D capture and digital twins of buildings, publishes blog posts on its own website about artificial intelligence in real estate. The material read covers two recurring posts, one on eight applications of AI in real estate and one on four use cases of AI in property management, each available in several language versions including Spanish, British English, Japanese, Italian, French, German and Korean. The posts are undated in the findings and are commercial in the sense that they promote Matterport's own Property Intelligence tools and customer examples.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The real estate post lists eight applications. It cites Delta Media reporting that over 87% of brokerages actively use AI tools, up 7% in the past year. It separates generative AI, which creates new content such as text, images and video from patterns learned in training data, from agentic AI, which performs tasks autonomously by making decisions or taking actions on the user's behalf, such as monitoring data streams, prioritising tasks, sending notifications or completing multi-step workflows. Generative AI powers listing descriptions and virtual staging, while agentic AI drives automation, decision support and proactive lead engagement. Property Intelligence tools provide generative AI services that automate manual listing tasks based on data captured from 3D property scans, or digital twins. Predictive models process large volumes of real estate data to uncover patterns for pricing. Smart assistants acknowledge inquiries instantly and keep communication moving until an agent steps in, and AI search categorises listings by lifestyle factors such as amenities, safety metrics, upcoming developments, sustainability and climate risk. The property management post covers tenant screening and risk calculations on ability to pay, maintenance trackers and predictive checks, pricing and ROI analysis, account reconciliation, chatbots and security monitoring, with customer examples from PlanOmatic and ID Plans.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source cites Delta Media for the claim that over 87% of brokerages are actively using AI tools, up by 7% in the past year. It says PlanOmatic used Matterport digital twins and AI-generated floor plans to perform remote inspections anywhere in the world, saving trips to more than 400,000 properties. It says ID Plans has spent more than 23 years helping commercial property managers with building configurations. It defines generative AI as creating new content from training data and agentic AI as acting autonomously on the user's behalf.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in real estate gets a vendor's structured map of where the technology is being applied, from listing content and virtual staging through pricing models, lead response and search, to back-office property management tasks such as screening, maintenance and reconciliation. The distinction between generative and agentic AI is a useful frame for sorting tools that produce content from tools that take actions. The Property Intelligence description is the clearest statement of how 3D scans and digital twins become the data layer that generative services draw on, which is the role Matterport itself plays in the industry.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: The posts are marketing content for Matterport's own products, and the customer examples, PlanOmatic and ID Plans, are Matterport customers. The findings give no publication dates, so the currency of the 87% figure and the 7% increase cannot be checked from the text. The material is a list of applications rather than original research, and the only outside statistic is attributed to Delta Media rather than gathered by Matterport. Several language versions repeat the same content, so the volume of pages overstates the amount of distinct information.
